title: Terence Tao
wiki_lead:
Terence Chi-Shen Tao  (Chinese: 陶哲轩; pinyin: Táo Zhéxuān; born 17 July 1975) is an Australian-American mathematician known for his contributions to partial differential equations, combinatorics, harmonic analysis and additive number theory. He was awarded the Fields Medal in 2006 for his contributions to mathematical analysis, discrete mathematics and pure mathematics. He is regarded by many as "the finest mathematician of his generation". 
Born to Chinese immigrant parents, Tao was raised in Adelaide, Australia. A child prodigy, he began competing in the International Mathematical Olympiad at age 10 and  became the youngest gold medallist in the history of the competition in 1988 at age 13. After earning his doctorate from Princeton University at age 21, he became the youngest full professor in the history of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), where he currently holds the James and Carol Collins Chair in Mathematics.  
Tao has made significant contributions to several branches of mathematics, including his collaboration with Ben Green on the Green–Tao theorem, which established that the prime numbers contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, and his work with Emmanuel Candès on the mathematical foundations of compressed sensing. His  honours include a MacArthur Fellowship (2007), the Crafoord Prize (2012), the Royal Medal (2014), and the Breakthrough Prize in Mathematics (2015). He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2007 and appointed a Companion of the Order of Australia in 2026.

Early life
Terence Chi-Shen Tao was born on 17 July 1975 in Adelaide, South Australia. His father, Billy Tao, was a Chinese paediatrician from Shanghai, China, while his mother, Grace Leong, was born in Hong Kong. His parents met while studying at the University of Hong Kong and emigrated to Australia in 1972. His mother received a first-class honours degree in mathematics and physics from the university. She taught science, physics, chemistry and mathematics at secondary schools in Hong Kong and Australia. Tao is the eldest of three sons, with two younger brothers: Trevor and Nigel. His younger brothers formerly represented Australia at the International Mathematical Olympiad.


Mathematics prodigy
A child prodigy, Tao exhibited extraordinary mathematical abilities when he was two years old. By the age of six, he had taught himself the programming language BASIC and had written computer programs involving Euclid's algorithm, Fibonacci numbers and prime numbers. He skipped five grades during primary school. He began attending Blackwood High School at age 7. His acceleration differed between academic subjects: at eight, he studied subjects such as English and physical education at Year 8 level, while his mathematics classes were at Year 11 or 12 level.
